## TL;DR

A blueberry flower's anthers open only through two small pores at the tip, and shed pollen only when vibrated at the right frequency, which is why bumblebees, not honeybees, are the more efficient pollinator. Many cultivars are also self-incompatible, setting little fruit from their own pollen, and berries from well-pollinated flowers end up both more numerous and larger, because seed number and berry size are linked.
:::

## A flower built to withhold its pollen

Most flowers shed pollen from anthers that split open along a seam as soon as they mature. A blueberry flower's anthers instead form two narrow tubes, each closed except for a pore at the tip, and pollen only falls out when something shakes the flower hard enough to jolt it loose through those pores. This is buzz pollination, and it is not incidental: it means an insect that cannot vibrate at the right frequency leaves with little or no pollen, and a flower is not raided empty by every passing visitor.

Bumblebees and several solitary bees can detach their flight muscles from their wings and vibrate their thorax directly against the anthers, a technique honeybees cannot perform. Where growers rely on rented honeybee hives alone, pollination is measurably less efficient per visit than where bumblebees or solitary bees are present, which is why many commercial plantings deliberately bring in bumblebee colonies alongside honeybee hives rather than one or the other.

## Why the flower needs a different plant, not just a visit

Many highbush blueberry cultivars are partly or largely self-incompatible: a flower's own pollen, or pollen from a genetically identical plant, fertilises few of its ovules even when it is delivered. A single-cultivar block, however well visited by bees, can set poorly for this reason alone. Commercial plantings interplant two or more compatible cultivars, or rely on nearby wild pollen sources, specifically so that cross-pollen is what the bees are actually moving between visits.

The payoff for good cross-pollination is not just more fruit; it is bigger fruit. Each ovule that gets fertilised develops into a seed, and a developing seed releases hormones that recruit surrounding tissue growth, so a berry with more fertilised ovules grows larger fruit flesh around them. Poorly pollinated flowers tend to abort or set small, sparsely seeded berries, which is why pollination quality shows up later as a size distribution, not only a fruit count.

## Key takeaways

- Blueberry anthers release pollen only through two tip pores under vibration; bumblebees and some solitary bees buzz-pollinate efficiently, honeybees cannot.
- Many cultivars are self-incompatible, so cross-pollen from a genetically different cultivar is needed for good fruit set, not just any pollinator visit.
- Seed number and berry size are linked, because each fertilised ovule recruits growth into the surrounding fruit tissue.
- A successfully fertilised flower now has ovules to grow around; the next module follows what those cells do first.
